```{r setup, include=FALSE}
needed_packages <- c("knitr", "ggplot2", "jsonlite", "digest")
available <- vapply(needed_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
if (!all(available)) stop("Install these packages first: ",
                          paste(needed_packages[!available], collapse = ", "))
library(ggplot2)
# Locate this file whether it is knitted or run chunk by chunk. When chunks are
# run by hand knitr::current_input() is NULL, and a personal .Rprofile may have
# changed the working directory at startup, so neither can be relied on alone.
resolve_analysis_dir <- function() {
  input <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
  if (length(input) == 1L && !is.na(input) && nzchar(input)) {
    return(normalizePath(dirname(input), winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE))
  }
  if (requireNamespace("rstudioapi", quietly = TRUE) &&
      isTRUE(try(rstudioapi::isAvailable(), silent = TRUE))) {
    open_file <- try(rstudioapi::getSourceEditorContext()$path, silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(open_file, "try-error") && length(open_file) == 1L &&
        nzchar(open_file)) {
      return(normalizePath(dirname(open_file), winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE))
    }
  }
  here <- normalizePath(getwd(), winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
  for (level in 1:6) {
    if (file.exists(file.path(here, "audit/source_manifest.json")) &&
        dir.exists(file.path(here, "data/raw")) &&
        dir.exists(file.path(here, "analysis"))) {
      return(file.path(here, "analysis"))
    }
    up <- dirname(here)
    if (identical(up, here)) break
    here <- up
  }
  stop("Cannot locate the project folder. The working directory is '", getwd(),
       "'. Either knit this file, or run setwd() to the project folder (the one ",
       "holding audit/ and data/) before running these chunks. A personal ",
       ".Rprofile containing setwd() will redirect the session at startup.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
analysis_dir <- resolve_analysis_dir()
project_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(analysis_dir, ".."), winslash = "/",
                             mustWork = TRUE)
artifact_dir <- file.path(analysis_dir, "artifacts")
dir.create(artifact_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = analysis_dir)
# Knitting is governed by root.dir above; an interactive session needs the
# working directory moved so that both routes behave the same way.
if (is.null(knitr::current_input())) setwd(analysis_dir)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.8, dpi = 150,
                      fig.path = "figures/", dev = "png", cache = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
set.seed(20261020)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
            theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
                  plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)))
show_table <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  knitr::kable(x, format = "pipe", digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

## 1. Purpose and current scope

This is the main analysis file for the project. All preprocessing and statistical analyses are written here, section by section. The current version completes preprocessing, exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the initial training set, and the logistic regression baseline with its diagnostics and validation scores. It does not score either 2025 test set; those partitions are read for structural checks only and stay unscored until the specification is frozen in section 9.

The outcome is whether the blue-side team wins a game. The prediction time is 15 minutes. The four predictors are blue-minus-red differences in gold, kills, experience points, and creep score. Creep score counts minions and monsters killed. A game is one observation; the two teams in a game are not independent observations.

The three research questions concern the relationship between early advantages and winning, differences across game patches, and prediction in a later year and another league. Patch means the recorded game version. These are observational data, so an association does not establish a causal effect.

The course folder does not currently contain lecture notes for this capstone. The instructor's proposal feedback and the revised analysis plan guide this file. The historical ten-question list is not the current analysis specification.

## 2. Sources and decisions made before analysis

The raw files are the saved September 2026 snapshot from [ChainCC](https://chaincc.lol/free/data). The provider's [methodology](https://chaincc.lol/about/methodology) lists several upstream sources. We use the local snapshot rather than silently downloading a newer version. File-year labels do not always equal the actual year of every game; we select games using the recorded match date.

A previous source check compared 11 selected training games with Games of Legends, covering eight patches, extreme gold differences, and one zero creep-score difference. All 44 early-feature comparisons agreed. Dates, sides, results, patch numbers, and durations also agreed. See the [source-check report](../07_数据来源抽查记录.md) for game links and evidence. This purposeful sample does not verify every record, and the websites may share upstream errors.

We retain the following decisions from the approved design:

- Keep one blue-side record per paired game and define every difference as blue minus red.
- Exclude games with invalid early measurements. The Chinese league in the original candidate pool has nonpositive early gold and is not used.
- Keep valid extreme values and genuine zero differences. Do not trim or winsorize them merely because they are unusual.
- Stop for unexpected missing values, duplicate keys, or new inconsistencies rather than silently filling values or choosing one duplicate.
- Preserve raw team names and team IDs. Record known historical display-name differences separately; do not automatically merge team identities across years.
- Keep the fixed chronological and geographic splits. Learn centering and scaling only from the current training set.

These decisions are not chosen by comparing model performance. Any later change that alters the cohort, outcome, or split must be recorded here before final testing.

## 3. Data preprocessing in R

### 3.1 Verify and read the frozen files

We check each raw file against its saved SHA-256 hash. Reading identifiers and patch codes as text preserves values such as `14.10`. A changed file stops the analysis and requires a new data-version decision.

```{r verify-and-read}
manifest <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(project_dir, "audit/source_manifest.json"))
source_files <- manifest$files
raw_paths <- file.path(project_dir, gsub("\\", "/", source_files$file, fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(all(file.exists(raw_paths)))
actual_hash <- vapply(raw_paths, function(p) {
  digest::digest(file = p, algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)
}, character(1))
file_check <- data.frame(file = basename(raw_paths),
                         hash_matches = actual_hash == source_files$sha256)
stopifnot(all(file_check$hash_matches))
show_table(file_check)

raw_list <- lapply(raw_paths, function(p) {
  read.csv(gzfile(p), colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE,
           na.strings = c("", "NA"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
stopifnot(all(vapply(raw_list, function(x) identical(names(x), names(raw_list[[1]])),
                     logical(1))))
for (i in seq_along(raw_list)) raw_list[[i]]$source_file <- basename(raw_paths[i])
raw <- do.call(rbind, raw_list)
rownames(raw) <- NULL
```

The three files contain `r format(nrow(raw), big.mark = ",")` team-game rows. This is not the number of independent games.

### 3.2 Check keys and select the original candidate pool

We use the date part of the source timestamp without converting time zones. The exact timestamp convention has not been independently verified. This preserves the recorded calendar dates used in the frozen split. We do not use the filename or the source `year` field to assign years.

```{r keys-and-candidates}
numeric_fields <- c("gamelength", "goldat10", "goldat15", "golddiffat10",
                    "golddiffat15", "xpdiffat10", "xpdiffat15",
                    "csdiffat10", "csdiffat15", "killsat15", "deathsat15")
required_raw <- c("game_id", "date", "league", "patch", "side", "team_id",
                  "team_name", "result", "game_number", numeric_fields)
stopifnot(all(required_raw %in% names(raw)),
          !anyNA(raw[c("game_id", "side")]),
          all(raw$side %in% c("Blue", "Red")))
key <- paste(raw$game_id, raw$side, sep = "|")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(key), all(table(raw$game_id) == 2L))
raw$match_date <- as.Date(substr(raw$date, 1, 10))
stopifnot(!anyNA(raw$match_date))
candidate <- raw[format(raw$match_date, "%Y") %in% c("2024", "2025") &
                   raw$league %in% c("LCK", "LEC", "LPL"), ]
missing_required <- vapply(candidate[required_raw], function(x) {
  sum(is.na(x) | trimws(x) == "")
}, integer(1))
stopifnot(all(missing_required == 0L))
stopifnot(all(candidate$result %in% c("TRUE", "FALSE")))
candidate$result <- as.integer(candidate$result == "TRUE")
for (v in numeric_fields) {
  candidate[[v]] <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(candidate[[v]]))
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(candidate[[v]])))
}
candidate$game_number <- as.integer(candidate$game_number)
stopifnot(!anyNA(candidate$game_number))
```

Here `LCK` means League of Legends Champions Korea; `LEC` means League of Legends EMEA Championship, where EMEA refers to Europe, the Middle East and Africa; and `LPL` means League of Legends Pro League in China. The retained analysis uses the Korean and European regional leagues.

### 3.3 Pair sides and apply the recorded quality rules

We match the red record to the blue record by game ID. The one-unit tolerance below reproduces the previous audit's rounding check. Missing cells have already been checked, so no imputation is applied. The old audit checked both 10- and 15-minute snapshots; keeping that rule preserves the frozen cohort even though the main prediction time is 15 minutes.

Deaths can exceed opposing kills because an execution need not give a player kill credit. We therefore do not require deaths to equal opposing kills. We flag the reverse inconsistency, where kills exceed the opponent's deaths.

```{r pair-and-check}
blue <- candidate[candidate$side == "Blue", ]
red <- candidate[candidate$side == "Red", ]
red <- red[match(blue$game_id, red$game_id), ]
stopifnot(identical(blue$game_id, red$game_id),
          !anyDuplicated(blue$game_id), nrow(blue) == nrow(red))
diff_fields <- c("golddiffat10", "golddiffat15", "xpdiffat10",
                 "xpdiffat15", "csdiffat10", "csdiffat15")
flags <- data.frame(
  noncomplementary_result = blue$result + red$result != 1,
  nonpositive_early_gold = blue$goldat10 <= 0 | red$goldat10 <= 0 |
                           blue$goldat15 <= 0 | red$goldat15 <= 0,
  too_short = blue$gamelength <= 900 | red$gamelength <= 900,
  inconsistent_context = blue$date != red$date | blue$league != red$league |
                          blue$patch != red$patch | blue$gamelength != red$gamelength,
  nonopposite_differences = Reduce(`|`, lapply(diff_fields, function(v) {
    abs(blue[[v]] + red[[v]]) > 1
  })),
  inconsistent_gold = abs(blue$goldat15 - red$goldat15 - blue$golddiffat15) > 1 |
                       abs(blue$goldat10 - red$goldat10 - blue$golddiffat10) > 1,
  impossible_kill_count = blue$killsat15 > red$deathsat15 |
                           red$killsat15 > blue$deathsat15,
  identical_team_ids = blue$team_id == red$team_id
)
excluded <- rowSums(flags) > 0
quality_table <- data.frame(check = names(flags), flagged_games = colSums(flags))
show_table(quality_table)
flow_by_league <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(blue$league)), function(lg) {
  ix <- blue$league == lg
  data.frame(league = lg, candidate_games = sum(ix),
             excluded_games = sum(ix & excluded), retained_games = sum(ix & !excluded))
}))
show_table(flow_by_league)
exclusion_ledger <- cbind(blue[c("game_id", "league", "match_date")], flags,
                         excluded = excluded)
# Stop if the exclusions differ from the previously audited snapshot.
stopifnot(nrow(blue) == 3159L, sum(excluded) == 1522L,
          all(blue$league[excluded] == "LPL"),
          all(flags$nonpositive_early_gold[excluded]))
```

All `r sum(excluded)` excluded candidate games are from the Chinese league and have invalid early gold. Zero-filled early statistics in these games cannot be treated as tied early states. This exclusion limits geographic scope; it is not evidence about that league's match performance. The table counts rule flags separately, so flags should not be added together as independent exclusions.

### 3.4 Construct one analysis row per game

The outcome is coded as 1 for a blue win and 0 for a blue loss. Gold, experience and creep-score differences are supplied by the source and have been checked against the paired records. The kill difference is calculated from the two teams' kill counts at 15 minutes. Final-game totals and game duration are not predictors.

```{r construct-analysis-data}
games <- data.frame(
  game_id = blue$game_id, match_date = blue$match_date,
  source_timestamp = blue$date, league = blue$league, patch = blue$patch,
  game_number = blue$game_number,
  blue_team_id = blue$team_id, red_team_id = red$team_id,
  blue_team_name_raw = blue$team_name, red_team_name_raw = red$team_name,
  blue_win = blue$result,
  gold15 = blue$golddiffat15,
  kills15 = blue$killsat15 - red$killsat15,
  experience15 = blue$xpdiffat15,
  creep15 = blue$csdiffat15,
  source_file = blue$source_file,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)[!excluded, ]
games <- games[order(games$match_date, games$source_timestamp, games$game_id), ]
rownames(games) <- NULL
features <- c("gold15", "kills15", "experience15", "creep15")
stopifnot(nrow(games) == 1637L, !anyDuplicated(games$game_id),
          !anyNA(games), all(games$league %in% c("LCK", "LEC")),
          all(games$blue_win %in% 0:1))
natural_key <- paste(games$league, games$source_timestamp,
                     pmin(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id),
                     pmax(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id), games$game_number)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(natural_key))
day_pair_key <- paste(games$league, games$match_date,
                      pmin(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id),
                      pmax(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id), games$game_number)
ambiguous_day_key <- duplicated(day_pair_key) | duplicated(day_pair_key, fromLast = TRUE)
day_key_review <- games[ambiguous_day_key,
                        c("game_id", "source_timestamp", "league", "game_number")]
stopifnot(all(games$league[ambiguous_day_key] == "LEC"),
          all(format(games$match_date[ambiguous_day_key], "%Y") == "2024"))

# Verify the reconstruction against the earlier frozen cohort; do not replace it.
frozen <- readRDS(file.path(project_dir, "data/derived/eligible_games.rds"))
stopifnot(setequal(games$game_id, frozen$game_id))
frozen <- frozen[match(games$game_id, frozen$game_id), ]
old_fields <- c("golddiffat15", "killdiffat15", "xpdiffat15", "csdiffat15")
for (i in seq_along(features)) {
  stopifnot(all(games[[features[i]]] == frozen[[old_fields[i]]]))
}
stopifnot(all(games$blue_win == as.integer(frozen$result)))
```

A date-only duplicate check finds two pairs of European 2024 records with the same day, team pair, and game number, but different IDs and timestamps. These are outside model development. We retain and flag them rather than assuming they are duplicates; their event identity has not been independently resolved. The primary key remains game ID, and the timestamp-based context key has no duplicates. A calendar date and game number alone are not a safe deletion rule.

```{r ambiguous-day-keys}
show_table(day_key_review)
```

```{r variable-dictionary}
dictionary <- data.frame(
  variable = c("blue_win", features, "patch", "match_date", "league",
               "blue_team_id / red_team_id", "game_id"),
  meaning = c("Final blue-side victory: 1 win, 0 loss",
              "Blue minus red gold at 15 minutes",
              "Blue kills minus red kills at 15 minutes",
              "Blue minus red experience at 15 minutes",
              "Blue minus red creep score at 15 minutes",
              "Recorded game-version code", "Recorded calendar date",
              "Competition code", "Source team identifiers", "Source game identifier"),
  unit_or_type = c("Binary", "Gold", "Kills", "Experience points", "CS count",
                   "Text/group", "Date", "Categorical", "Text", "Text"),
  role = c("Outcome", rep("Predictor", 4), "Later hierarchical grouping",
           "Split and dependence checks", "Split only", "Coverage/dependence checks", "Pairing/key")
)
show_table(dictionary)
```

The source check found historical display-name differences for DN SOOPers/Kwangdong Freecs and HANJIN BRION/OK BRION. We preserve raw names in this file and use IDs for counting teams. No team-name correction is used as a model feature. These specific matches do not validate every historical team identity.

## 4. Training, validation and test design

We use a chronological split within the Korean league. Games from January through June 2024 form the initial training set. Games from July through September 2024 form the validation set. This asks whether choices made with earlier games remain useful for later games from the same league. It also reduces leakage that would arise from randomly mixing earlier and later games.

There are two separate 2025 test sets. Korean games measure transfer to a later year within the source league. European regional games measure transfer to another league and a later year. European games from 2024 remain outside model development. All matches from the same series occur within one partition under these date rules; we verify that property below.

After model settings are chosen using only training and validation data, we will refit the selected recipe on all 482 Korean games from 2024. This is the union of training and validation, not an extra independent dataset. Both 2025 tests remain outside preprocessing choices, tuning, prior selection, cluster-count selection, and calibration adjustments.

```{r define-fixed-splits}
games$partition <- NA_character_
games$partition[games$league == "LCK" & games$match_date >= as.Date("2024-01-01") &
                  games$match_date < as.Date("2024-07-01")] <- "train"
games$partition[games$league == "LCK" & games$match_date >= as.Date("2024-07-01") &
                  games$match_date < as.Date("2024-10-01")] <- "validation"
games$partition[games$league == "LCK" & format(games$match_date, "%Y") == "2025"] <- "test_time"
games$partition[games$league == "LEC" & format(games$match_date, "%Y") == "2025"] <- "test_external"
games$partition[games$league == "LEC" & format(games$match_date, "%Y") == "2024"] <- "unused"
partition_order <- c("train", "validation", "test_time", "test_external", "unused")
stopifnot(!anyNA(games$partition))
split_ids <- lapply(partition_order, function(p) games$game_id[games$partition == p])
names(split_ids) <- partition_order
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(lengths(split_ids)), c(313L, 169L, 555L, 306L, 294L)))
old_ids <- readRDS(file.path(project_dir, "audit/proposed_teacher_split_ids.rds"))
stopifnot(all(vapply(seq_along(split_ids), function(i) {
  setequal(split_ids[[i]], old_ids[[i]])
}, logical(1))))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unlist(split_ids, use.names = FALSE)))
# Conservative series proxy: same date, league and unordered pair of teams.
series_proxy <- paste(games$league, games$match_date,
                      pmin(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id),
                      pmax(games$blue_team_id, games$red_team_id))
stopifnot(all(vapply(split(games$partition, series_proxy), function(p) {
  length(unique(p)) == 1L
}, logical(1))))
train <- games[games$partition == "train", ]
validation <- games[games$partition == "validation", ]
test_time <- games[games$partition == "test_time", ]
test_external <- games[games$partition == "test_external", ]
unused <- games[games$partition == "unused", ]
week_start <- function(date) as.Date(cut(date, "weeks", start.on.monday = TRUE))
partition_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(partition_order, function(p) {
  z <- games[games$partition == p, ]
  data.frame(partition = p, games = nrow(z), first_date = min(z$match_date),
             last_date = max(z$match_date), patches = length(unique(z$patch)),
             observed_weeks = length(unique(week_start(z$match_date))))
}))
show_table(partition_table)
```

The table describes the saved data's actual coverage, not a claim that every official game is present. A same-day team-pair proxy is not a complete official series identifier, but the chronological boundaries keep these groups together. Teams recur over many games and weeks, so a date split does not make observations independent.

The validation set has `r length(setdiff(unique(validation$patch), unique(train$patch)))` patches not seen in training. Every 2025 test patch is new relative to the 2024 Korean source data. This matters for the later Bayesian model: predictions must average over uncertainty for unseen patch effects, rather than estimate those effects using held-out outcomes.

```{r verify-new-patches}
source_patches <- union(train$patch, validation$patch)
stopifnot(length(source_patches) == 12L,
          length(intersect(unique(test_time$patch), source_patches)) == 0L,
          length(intersect(unique(test_external$patch), source_patches)) == 0L)
```

Only dates, identifiers, patch coverage, and structural validity are checked outside training here. We do not calculate validation or test win rates, predictor-outcome associations, or prediction scores.

### 4.1 Fit preprocessing parameters using training data only

We keep the original units and add standardized copies for later methods that need them. A standardized value subtracts the training mean and divides by the training standard deviation. This is particularly useful for clustering and for expressing Bayesian priors on comparable scales. It is not essential for a random forest.

There is no imputation, outlier removal, feature selection, or outcome-based transformation in this step. Future final refitting will recompute the same recipe on the 482-game source set, only after choices have been frozen.

```{r training-only-scaling}
scaling <- data.frame(variable = features,
                      center = vapply(train[features], mean, numeric(1)),
                      scale = vapply(train[features], sd, numeric(1)), row.names = NULL)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(scaling$scale)), all(scaling$scale > 0))
apply_scaling <- function(d, recipe) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(recipe))) {
    v <- recipe$variable[i]
    d[[paste0(v, "_z")]] <- (d[[v]] - recipe$center[i]) / recipe$scale[i]
  }
  d
}
train <- apply_scaling(train, scaling)
validation <- apply_scaling(validation, scaling)
test_time <- apply_scaling(test_time, scaling)
test_external <- apply_scaling(test_external, scaling)
show_table(scaling)
stopifnot(all(abs(vapply(train[paste0(features, "_z")], mean, numeric(1))) < 1e-10),
          all(abs(vapply(train[paste0(features, "_z")], sd, numeric(1)) - 1) < 1e-10))
```

## 5. Training-set exploratory analysis

Every table, figure, and outcome summary in this section uses only the 313 initial training games. These are descriptive findings for developing the analysis; they are not held-out performance results or causal conclusions.

### 5.1 Size, outcome balance and repeated teams

```{r training-overview}
train$week <- week_start(train$match_date)
overview <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("Games", "Blue wins", "Blue losses", "Unique team IDs",
               "Patches", "Observed calendar weeks"),
  value = c(nrow(train), sum(train$blue_win), sum(1 - train$blue_win),
            length(unique(c(train$blue_team_id, train$red_team_id))),
            length(unique(train$patch)), length(unique(train$week)))
)
show_table(overview, digits = 0)
team_appearances <- table(c(train$blue_team_id, train$red_team_id))
```

The training data cover `r min(train$match_date)` through `r max(train$match_date)`. Blue won `r sum(train$blue_win)` of `r nrow(train)` games (`r pct(mean(train$blue_win))`). The outcome classes are reasonably balanced, so there is no current reason to oversample a class. This proportion does not establish a causal blue-side advantage.

There are `r length(team_appearances)` team IDs, with `r min(team_appearances)` to `r max(team_appearances)` game appearances per team. Repeated teams and games within series create dependence. The later uncertainty analysis must address this limitation; treating all 313 games as fully independent would be too strong.

### 5.2 Coverage over weeks and patches

```{r weekly-coverage}
weekly <- aggregate(list(games = train$game_id), list(week = train$week), length)
calendar <- data.frame(week = seq(min(train$week), max(train$week), by = "week"))
weekly <- merge(calendar, weekly, by = "week", all.x = TRUE)
weekly$games[is.na(weekly$games)] <- 0L
ggplot(weekly, aes(week, games)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#286B8E", width = 5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(title = "Training coverage by calendar week", x = NULL, y = "Games",
       caption = "Zero bars mean no retained games in that week; they do not identify the reason.")
```

```{r patch-coverage}
patch_counts <- as.data.frame(table(train$patch), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(patch_counts) <- c("patch", "games")
ggplot(patch_counts, aes(patch, games)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#286B8E") + geom_text(aes(label = games), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Training games per recorded patch", x = "Patch", y = "Games")
```

There are `r nrow(patch_counts)` training patches, with `r min(patch_counts$games)` to `r max(patch_counts$games)` games per patch. Patch coverage is uneven. This supports partial pooling as a model to investigate, but eight training groups give limited information about between-patch variation, especially random slopes. Gaps in the weekly figure should not automatically be called missing data; checking full official schedule coverage is outside this EDA.

### 5.3 Predictor distributions and unusual values

```{r predictor-summary}
feature_labels <- c(gold15 = "Gold difference", kills15 = "Kill difference",
                    experience15 = "Experience difference", creep15 = "Creep-score difference")
summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  x <- train[[v]]
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]), n = length(x), missing = sum(is.na(x)),
             mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), minimum = min(x),
             q25 = unname(quantile(x, 0.25)), median = median(x),
             q75 = unname(quantile(x, 0.75)), maximum = max(x), zero_count = sum(x == 0))
}))
show_table(summary_table)
long_train <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  data.frame(game_id = train$game_id, variable = unname(feature_labels[v]),
             value = train[[v]], standardized = train[[paste0(v, "_z")]],
             outcome = factor(train$blue_win, levels = 0:1, labels = c("Blue loss", "Blue win")))
}))
```

```{r predictor-distributions, fig.height=6}
continuous <- long_train[long_train$variable != "Kill difference", ]
discrete <- long_train[long_train$variable == "Kill difference", ]
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(data = continuous, bins = 24, fill = "#286B8E", color = "white") +
  geom_histogram(data = discrete, binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5,
                 fill = "#286B8E", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#923A31") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of the four early differences", x = "Blue minus red", y = "Games",
       caption = "Panels use different units and axis ranges. The dashed line marks an equal value.")
```

Gold differences range from `r min(train$gold15)` to `r max(train$gold15)`, and kill differences range from `r min(train$kills15)` to `r max(train$kills15)`. A negative value means the blue team is behind on that measure. Equal values are possible and do not automatically indicate missingness.

We flag values outside the usual 1.5-interquartile-range (IQR) fences for inspection. An IQR flag is not a measurement-error rule and is not a regression influence diagnostic. We retain these games. The source audit already checked the largest and smallest training gold differences against external records.

```{r unusual-values-no-removal}
iqr_checks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  x <- train[[v]]
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75))
  lower <- unname(q[1] - 1.5 * IQR(x))
  upper <- unname(q[2] + 1.5 * IQR(x))
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]), lower_fence = lower,
             upper_fence = upper, flagged_games = sum(x < lower | x > upper),
             removed_games = 0L)
}))
show_table(iqr_checks)
```

### 5.4 Correlation and redundancy among predictors

```{r predictor-correlations}
cor_matrix <- cor(train[features], method = "pearson")
dimnames(cor_matrix) <- list(unname(feature_labels[features]), unname(feature_labels[features]))
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(cor_long) <- c("x", "y", "correlation")
ggplot(cor_long, aes(x, y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#B84735", mid = "white", high = "#5298B9",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Pearson correlations in the training set", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation")
```

Gold and experience differences have a correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", cor(train$gold15, train$experience15))`; gold and kill differences have a correlation of `r sprintf("%.3f", cor(train$gold15, train$kills15))`. Several indicators describe related aspects of the early state. A later regression coefficient will describe a conditional association, holding the other predictors fixed. These correlations may make individual coefficients less stable, even if prediction remains useful. We do not remove a variable using an arbitrary correlation cutoff at this stage.

### 5.5 Gold difference and observed win frequency

For an easy-to-read descriptive plot, we use fixed 2,000-gold bands with open-ended tails. These cut points are display choices, not new model predictors or boundaries selected to maximize a relationship. Games at zero are in the 0 to 2,000 band. Counts are displayed because tail bands contain fewer games.

```{r gold-bands-table}
gold_labels <- c("< -4000", "[-4000, -2000)", "[-2000, 0)",
                 "[0, 2000)", "[2000, 4000)", ">= 4000")
train$gold_band <- cut(train$gold15,
                       breaks = c(-Inf, -4000, -2000, 0, 2000, 4000, Inf),
                       labels = gold_labels, right = FALSE)
gold_bands <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(train$gold_band), function(band) {
  z <- train[train$gold_band == band, ]
  data.frame(band = band, games = nrow(z), blue_wins = sum(z$blue_win),
             blue_win_fraction = mean(z$blue_win))
}))
gold_bands$band <- factor(gold_bands$band, levels = gold_labels)
show_table(gold_bands, digits = 3)
```

```{r gold-bands-plot}
ggplot(gold_bands, aes(band, blue_win_fraction)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#286B8E") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", games)), vjust = -1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%"),
                     limits = c(0, 1.12), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Observed blue win frequency by early gold difference",
       x = "Gold difference at 15 minutes (blue minus red)", y = "Observed blue win fraction",
       caption = "Training data only. Unadjusted descriptive fractions, not a fitted probability model.")
```

The lowest band contains `r gold_bands$games[1]` games, with `r gold_bands$blue_wins[1]` blue wins (`r pct(gold_bands$blue_win_fraction[1])`). The highest band contains `r tail(gold_bands$games, 1)` games, with `r tail(gold_bands$blue_wins, 1)` blue wins (`r pct(tail(gold_bands$blue_win_fraction, 1))`). This comparison is unadjusted and the tail samples are small. It does not tell us how much gold independently changes the chance of winning or how well a model will predict new games. No confidence intervals or significance tests are claimed for these fractions.

### 5.6 Predictor distributions by final outcome

```{r outcome-boxplots, fig.height=6}
ggplot(long_train, aes(outcome, standardized, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Blue loss" = "#AAB8C2", "Blue win" = "#5298B9")) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Early states in games later won or lost by blue",
       x = NULL, y = "Training-standardized difference",
       caption = "The zero line is the training mean, not necessarily equality between teams.")
```

```{r outcome-median-summary}
outcome_medians <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]),
             median_blue_loss = median(train[[v]][train$blue_win == 0]),
             median_blue_win = median(train[[v]][train$blue_win == 1]))
}))
show_table(outcome_medians)
```

The median gold difference is `r outcome_medians$median_blue_loss[1]` in blue losses and `r outcome_medians$median_blue_win[1]` in blue wins. The plots show how the early distributions differ by the final outcome, but there is overlap. We will need held-out prediction and model checks before drawing conclusions about predictive value. Differences can also reflect unmeasured team strength, draft choices, and other game events.

### 5.7 Implications for the next analysis

The current data support starting with the planned four-predictor logistic regression. The classes are balanced and the predictor ranges are nonconstant. Correlated predictors require careful conditional interpretation. Extreme observations are retained for later influence checks. The small number of training patches limits how precisely a hierarchical model can estimate patch-specific slopes.

There is no evidence here that random forests outperform regression, that patches have different effects, or that clear clusters exist: those models have not been fitted. The validation data will support a limited set of choices, and the two tests will be evaluated only after the analysis recipe is frozen.

## 7. Logistic regression baseline

This section fits the first predictive model. Its settings come from the plan written before any model was fitted: the same four early differences, a binomial logistic link, and a reference forecast that predicts the training win proportion for every game. The 169 validation games are scored here. The two 2025 test sets are not read, scored, or summarized anywhere in this section.

### 7.1 Scoring code shared by every later model

These functions are defined once and reused by the later sections, so every model is judged by identical code. Log loss is the primary measure, with Brier score and calibration as support. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is supplementary: it measures ranking only and ignores whether the probabilities are numerically correct. The helpers are checked against cases whose answers can be worked out by hand.

```{r scoring-helpers}
log_loss <- function(y, p, eps = 1e-15) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(p, eps), 1 - eps)
  -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
}
brier_score <- function(y, p) mean((p - y)^2)
auc_roc <- function(y, p) {
  n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(rank(p)[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
score_predictions <- function(label, set, y, p) {
  data.frame(model = label, set = set, games = length(y),
             log_loss = log_loss(y, p), brier = brier_score(y, p),
             auc = auc_roc(y, p), mean_predicted = mean(p), observed = mean(y))
}
calibration_table <- function(y, p, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)) {
  bin <- cut(p, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(bin), function(b) {
    k <- which(bin == b)
    data.frame(bin = b, games = length(k),
               mean_predicted = if (length(k)) mean(p[k]) else NA_real_,
               observed = if (length(k)) mean(y[k]) else NA_real_)
  }))
}
stopifnot(abs(log_loss(c(1, 0), c(0.5, 0.5)) + log(0.5)) < 1e-12,
          brier_score(c(1, 0), c(1, 0)) == 0,
          abs(auc_roc(c(0, 0, 1, 1), c(0.1, 0.2, 0.8, 0.9)) - 1) < 1e-12,
          abs(auc_roc(c(0, 1), c(0.5, 0.5)) - 0.5) < 1e-12)
```

### 7.2 Baseline fit and reference forecast

The baseline keeps the predictors in their recorded units, so each coefficient refers to a one-unit change in that measure. The reference forecast uses the training win proportion and ignores the predictors; it is the honest no-information comparison, and it is never computed from validation or test outcomes.

```{r baseline-fit}
stopifnot(nrow(train) == 313L, nrow(validation) == 169L)
baseline_formula <- blue_win ~ gold15 + kills15 + experience15 + creep15
baseline <- glm(baseline_formula, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = train)
reference_rate <- mean(train$blue_win)
stopifnot(isTRUE(baseline$converged), !isTRUE(baseline$boundary))
coef_summary <- summary(baseline)$coefficients
wald_ci <- confint.default(baseline)
coef_table <- data.frame(
  term = rownames(coef_summary), estimate = coef_summary[, "Estimate"],
  std_error = coef_summary[, "Std. Error"], z_value = coef_summary[, "z value"],
  p_value = coef_summary[, "Pr(>|z|)"], ci_low = wald_ci[, 1],
  ci_high = wald_ci[, 2], row.names = NULL)
show_table(coef_table, digits = 5)
```

Coefficients on recorded units are very small numbers for gold and experience, so the next table restates each one over a step that is easier to read. An odds ratio above one means larger values of that measure go with a higher estimated chance of a blue win, holding the other three fixed.

```{r baseline-steps}
steps <- c(gold15 = 1000, kills15 = 1, experience15 = 1000, creep15 = 10)
step_labels <- c(gold15 = "per 1,000 gold", kills15 = "per 1 kill",
                 experience15 = "per 1,000 experience points",
                 creep15 = "per 10 creep score")
step_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  i <- match(v, coef_table$term)
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]), step = unname(step_labels[v]),
             log_odds_change = coef_table$estimate[i] * steps[[v]],
             odds_ratio = exp(coef_table$estimate[i] * steps[[v]]),
             ci_low = exp(coef_table$ci_low[i] * steps[[v]]),
             ci_high = exp(coef_table$ci_high[i] * steps[[v]]))
}))
show_table(step_table, digits = 3)
```

These are conditional associations in the training data. They do not say what would happen if a team were handed extra gold: the four measures move together, and all of them respond to unmeasured play quality, draft, and team strength.

Only the creep-score interval excludes an odds ratio of one (`r sprintf("%.3f", step_table$ci_low[4])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", step_table$ci_high[4])`). The gold, kill, and experience intervals all include one, and the intercept is near zero (`r sprintf("%.3f", coef_table$estimate[1])`), which matches the balanced training classes. Weak individual coefficients are not the same as a weak model: section 7.8 shows that the four predictors together score far better than the reference forecast. The next two subsections explain why the separate terms are hard to pin down.

### 7.3 Collinearity among the predictors

Section 5.4 showed strong correlations. The variance inflation factor restates that in terms of each coefficient's variance, so a value of 5 means the squared standard error is about five times what it would be if that predictor were uncorrelated with the others. It is computed here from the share of each predictor explained by the remaining three.

```{r collinearity-vif}
vif_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  r2 <- summary(lm(reformulate(setdiff(features, v), response = v), data = train))$r.squared
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]), r_squared_on_others = r2,
             vif = 1 / (1 - r2))
}))
show_table(vif_table, digits = 3)
design_sv <- svd(scale(as.matrix(train[features])))$d
condition_number <- max(design_sv) / min(design_sv)
```

Each predictor is between `r pct(min(vif_table$r_squared_on_others))` and `r pct(max(vif_table$r_squared_on_others))` explained by the other three, giving variance inflation factors from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(vif_table$vif))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(vif_table$vif))`; the gold term is the worst affected. The scaled design matrix has a condition number of `r sprintf("%.1f", condition_number)`, which is not extreme, so this is ordinary correlation among related measures rather than a numerically unstable fit. The practical consequence is that the model estimates the combined early advantage far more precisely than it can divide that advantage into four separate contributions. We keep all four predictors, as planned, and do not interpret any single coefficient on its own.

### 7.4 Separation and convergence

Section 5.5 showed that every training game with a gold difference of 4,000 or more was a blue win. If a single predictor split the outcomes completely, the maximum likelihood estimate would not exist, and the fit would drift toward extreme coefficients with very large standard errors. The checks below ask whether that happened.

```{r separation-checks}
fitted_train <- fitted(baseline)
separation_checks <- data.frame(
  check = c("Model reported convergence", "Fit reported at boundary",
            "Scoring iterations used", "Fitted probabilities below 0.001",
            "Fitted probabilities above 0.999",
            "Largest absolute coefficient estimate", "Largest standard error",
            "Largest absolute z value"),
  value = c(as.character(isTRUE(baseline$converged)),
            as.character(isTRUE(baseline$boundary)), as.character(baseline$iter),
            as.character(sum(fitted_train < 0.001)),
            as.character(sum(fitted_train > 0.999)),
            sprintf("%.5f", max(abs(coef_summary[, "Estimate"]))),
            sprintf("%.5f", max(coef_summary[, "Std. Error"])),
            sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(coef_summary[, "z value"])))))
show_table(separation_checks)
overlap_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  x <- train[[v]]
  data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]),
             max_among_blue_losses = max(x[train$blue_win == 0]),
             min_among_blue_wins = min(x[train$blue_win == 1]),
             ranges_overlap = min(x[train$blue_win == 1]) < max(x[train$blue_win == 0]))
}))
show_table(overlap_table, digits = 1)
```

There is no sign of separation. The fit converged in `r baseline$iter` iterations, no fitted probability falls below 0.001 or above 0.999, the largest standard error is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(coef_summary[, "Std. Error"]))`, and the largest absolute z value is `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(coef_summary[, "z value"])))`. For all four measures the ranges overlap between blue wins and blue losses: the largest gold difference in a blue loss is `r max(train$gold15[train$blue_win == 0])`, while the smallest in a blue win is `r min(train$gold15[train$blue_win == 1])`. The perfect win rates in the extreme bands of section 5.5 came from those wide bands and their small counts, not from a predictor that splits the outcomes.

### 7.5 Functional form

A logistic model with linear terms assumes each measure shifts the log odds at a constant rate. To check this we group games into ten equal-count bins for each predictor and average the response residual within each bin. Under the model these averages should scatter around zero. Bands of plus or minus two standard errors are shown; with forty bins in total a few excursions are expected by chance, so the plot is read for shape rather than for individual points.

```{r binned-residuals, fig.height=6}
residual_raw <- train$blue_win - fitted_train
binned_residuals <- do.call(rbind, lapply(features, function(v) {
  cuts <- unique(quantile(train[[v]], probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 11)))
  bin <- cut(train[[v]], cuts, include.lowest = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(bin), function(lev) {
    k <- which(bin == lev)
    data.frame(variable = unname(feature_labels[v]), games = length(k),
               mean_x = mean(train[[v]][k]), mean_residual = mean(residual_raw[k]),
               se = sd(residual_raw[k]) / sqrt(length(k)))
  }))
}))
ggplot(binned_residuals, aes(mean_x, mean_residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#923A31") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_residual - 2 * se, ymax = mean_residual + 2 * se),
                width = 0, color = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, color = "#286B8E") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Binned response residuals from the baseline model",
       x = "Bin mean of the predictor",
       y = "Bin mean residual (observed minus fitted)",
       caption = "Training data, ten equal-count bins per predictor. Bars span plus or minus two standard errors.")
flagged_bins <- binned_residuals[abs(binned_residuals$mean_residual) >
                                   2 * binned_residuals$se, ]
form_problem <- nrow(flagged_bins) > 0
```

The predeclared rule is that a spline term for gold is compared with the linear term, on validation only, if this check suggests a problem. The chunk below applies that rule instead of deciding after seeing the scores.

```{r predeclared-spline-rule}
if (form_problem) {
  spline_fit <- glm(blue_win ~ splines::ns(gold15, df = 3) + kills15 +
                      experience15 + creep15, family = binomial, data = train)
  spline_comparison <- rbind(
    score_predictions("Linear gold term", "validation", validation$blue_win,
                      predict(baseline, newdata = validation, type = "response")),
    score_predictions("Natural spline gold term, 3 degrees of freedom", "validation",
                      validation$blue_win,
                      predict(spline_fit, newdata = validation, type = "response")))
  show_table(spline_comparison, digits = 4)
} else {
  spline_comparison <- NULL
  cat("The functional-form check flagged no bin, so the predeclared spline",
      "comparison is not run and the linear form is kept.\n")
}
```

The check flagged `r nrow(flagged_bins)` of the `r nrow(binned_residuals)` bins: the gold bin centred on `r round(flagged_bins$mean_x[1])` gold, where the mean residual is `r sprintf("%.3f", flagged_bins$mean_residual[1])` against a standard error of `r sprintf("%.3f", flagged_bins$se[1])`. With `r nrow(binned_residuals)` bins and two-standard-error bands, about two flagged bins are expected by chance, so one is not evidence of a curved relationship. The rule as written triggers on any flagged bin, which is more sensitive than the plan intended; the comparison therefore ran, and it is reported above rather than dropped.

The spline improves validation log loss by `r sprintf("%.4f", spline_comparison$log_loss[1] - spline_comparison$log_loss[2])` on 169 games. That margin is far too small to establish a better functional form, and the week-block resampling planned for section 9 would produce differences of this size routinely. We keep the linear form for sections 8 and 9, which is also the plan's default. This decision is recorded before any test set is read.

### 7.6 Leverage and influential games

Leverage measures how unusual a game's predictor values are; Cook's distance measures how much the fitted coefficients would move if that game were dropped. Both are properties of the fit, not evidence that a game is wrong, and no game is removed. Instead the model is refitted without the flagged games to see whether any conclusion depends on them.

```{r influence-diagnostics}
leverage <- hatvalues(baseline)
cooks <- cooks.distance(baseline)
influence_cut <- 4 / nrow(train)
influential <- order(cooks, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
influence_table <- data.frame(
  game_id = train$game_id[influential], patch = train$patch[influential],
  gold15 = train$gold15[influential], kills15 = train$kills15[influential],
  blue_win = train$blue_win[influential],
  fitted_probability = fitted_train[influential],
  leverage = leverage[influential], cooks_distance = cooks[influential],
  row.names = NULL)
show_table(influence_table, digits = 4)
refit_without <- glm(baseline_formula, family = binomial,
                     data = train[cooks <= influence_cut, ])
coef_shift <- data.frame(
  variable = unname(feature_labels[features]),
  full_fit = coef(baseline)[features],
  refit_dropping_flagged = coef(refit_without)[features],
  relative_change = abs(coef(refit_without)[features] / coef(baseline)[features] - 1),
  row.names = NULL)
show_table(coef_shift, digits = 5)
```

No single game dominates the fit: the largest Cook's distance is `r sprintf("%.4f", max(cooks))` and the largest leverage is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(leverage))`, both well below the usual thresholds for concern. The refit nevertheless drops the `r sum(cooks > influence_cut)` games above the `r sprintf("%.4f", influence_cut)` screening value and moves the coefficients a long way: the kill coefficient changes sign, and the gold and experience coefficients change by `r pct(coef_shift$relative_change[1])` and `r pct(coef_shift$relative_change[3])`. This is the collinearity of section 7.3 seen from another angle. The combined prediction is stable while the split between correlated terms is not, which is a further reason to report predicted probabilities rather than individual coefficients.

### 7.7 Residual summaries by team and by week

Games are not independent: the same teams reappear across weeks, and the plan requires checking whether the model is systematically wrong for particular teams or periods. A residual is defined from each team's own point of view, so a team appearing on the red side contributes the negated blue-side residual.

```{r grouped-residuals}
team_view <- rbind(
  data.frame(team = train$blue_team_id, residual = residual_raw),
  data.frame(team = train$red_team_id, residual = -residual_raw))
team_residuals <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(team_view, team_view$team), function(z) {
  data.frame(team = z$team[1], games = nrow(z), mean_residual = mean(z$residual),
             se = sd(z$residual) / sqrt(nrow(z)))
}))
team_residuals <- team_residuals[order(-abs(team_residuals$mean_residual)), ]
team_residuals$outside_two_se <- abs(team_residuals$mean_residual) >
  2 * team_residuals$se
show_table(head(team_residuals, 6), digits = 3)
week_residuals <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(residual_raw, train$week), function(z) {
  data.frame(games = length(z), mean_residual = mean(z))
}))
week_residuals$week <- as.Date(rownames(week_residuals))
rownames(week_residuals) <- NULL
```

```{r week-residual-plot, fig.height=3.6}
ggplot(week_residuals, aes(week, mean_residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#923A31") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = week, yend = 0), color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(size = games), color = "#286B8E") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 4.5)) +
  labs(title = "Mean weekly residual from the baseline model", x = NULL,
       y = "Mean residual", size = "Games",
       caption = "Training weeks only. Point size shows how many games the week contributes.")
```

`r sum(team_residuals$outside_two_se)` of the `r nrow(team_residuals)` teams have a mean residual more than two standard errors from zero, the largest being `r sprintf("%+.3f", team_residuals$mean_residual[1])` over `r team_residuals$games[1]` games. A positive value means the team wins more often than its early statistics alone would suggest. Weekly means range from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(week_residuals$mean_residual))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(week_residuals$mean_residual))` across `r nrow(week_residuals)` training weeks. This is the expected trace of team strength, which the model deliberately does not measure. It is a limitation to report rather than something to repair with team indicators, which would not transfer to the 2025 test leagues. The predeclared week-effect sensitivity check in the plan is worth carrying out on source data before the specification is frozen.

### 7.8 Validation performance

The baseline and the reference forecast are now scored on the 169 validation games. In-sample training scores are shown for contrast only; they are optimistic because the coefficients were chosen using those games.

```{r validation-scores}
validation_p <- predict(baseline, newdata = validation, type = "response")
reference_p <- rep(reference_rate, nrow(validation))
score_table <- rbind(
  score_predictions("Four-predictor logistic regression", "training",
                    train$blue_win, fitted_train),
  score_predictions("Training win-rate reference", "training",
                    train$blue_win, rep(reference_rate, nrow(train))),
  score_predictions("Four-predictor logistic regression", "validation",
                    validation$blue_win, validation_p),
  score_predictions("Training win-rate reference", "validation",
                    validation$blue_win, reference_p))
show_table(score_table, digits = 4)
stopifnot(all(score_table$set %in% c("training", "validation")))
```

The baseline reaches a validation log loss of `r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[3])` against `r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[4])` for the reference, an improvement of `r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[4] - score_table$log_loss[3])`, with a validation area under the curve of `r sprintf("%.3f", score_table$auc[3])`. The gap between training and validation log loss is small (`r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[1])` against `r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[3])`), which is what a four-predictor linear model should do and leaves little room for overfitting. These validation numbers guided only the functional-form decision in 7.5; they are not held-out test results.

```{r validation-calibration, fig.height=4.2}
calibration <- calibration_table(validation$blue_win, validation_p)
show_table(calibration, digits = 3)
ggplot(calibration[!is.na(calibration$observed), ], aes(mean_predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey55") +
  geom_point(aes(size = games), color = "#286B8E") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", games)), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.2) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 5), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(title = "Validation calibration of the baseline model",
       x = "Mean predicted probability in bin", y = "Observed blue win fraction",
       caption = "169 validation games in fixed 0.2-wide bins. Bins hold few games, so the points are imprecise.")
```

Calibration is reasonable but imperfect. The middle bin's observed win fraction is `r sprintf("%.3f", calibration$observed[3])` against a mean prediction of `r sprintf("%.3f", calibration$mean_predicted[3])` on `r calibration$games[3]` games, and the top bin is `r sprintf("%.3f", calibration$observed[5])` against `r sprintf("%.3f", calibration$mean_predicted[5])` on `r calibration$games[5]` games, which hints at slight overconfidence at the high end. With `r min(calibration$games)` to `r max(calibration$games)` games per bin these deviations are imprecise, and no calibration adjustment is fitted here.

### 7.9 Estimated probabilities across the gold range

The curve below shows the estimated win probability as the gold difference varies, with the other three measures held at their training medians. It describes games that look like this in the training data. It is not the effect of changing one input while the others stay genuinely fixed, which rarely happens in a real game.

```{r probability-curve, fig.height=4.2}
contrast_grid <- data.frame(
  gold15 = seq(min(train$gold15), max(train$gold15), length.out = 120),
  kills15 = median(train$kills15), experience15 = median(train$experience15),
  creep15 = median(train$creep15))
link_fit <- predict(baseline, newdata = contrast_grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
contrast_grid$estimate <- plogis(link_fit$fit)
contrast_grid$ci_low <- plogis(link_fit$fit - 1.96 * link_fit$se.fit)
contrast_grid$ci_high <- plogis(link_fit$fit + 1.96 * link_fit$se.fit)
ggplot(contrast_grid, aes(gold15, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), fill = "#286B8E", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(color = "#286B8E", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_rug(data = train, aes(x = gold15, y = NULL), sides = "b", alpha = 0.3,
           color = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%"), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Estimated blue win probability across the training gold range",
       x = "Gold difference at 15 minutes (blue minus red)",
       y = "Estimated probability of a blue win",
       caption = "Other three measures held at training medians. The band is a 95% interval for the mean, not a prediction interval. The rug marks training games.")
probability_points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(-4000, -2000, 0, 2000, 4000), function(g) {
  row <- data.frame(gold15 = g, kills15 = median(train$kills15),
                    experience15 = median(train$experience15),
                    creep15 = median(train$creep15))
  lk <- predict(baseline, newdata = row, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
  data.frame(gold_difference = g, estimate = plogis(lk$fit),
             ci_low = plogis(lk$fit - 1.96 * lk$se.fit),
             ci_high = plogis(lk$fit + 1.96 * lk$se.fit),
             training_games_within_500 = sum(abs(train$gold15 - g) <= 500),
             row.names = NULL)
}))
show_table(probability_points, digits = 3)
```

Holding the other three measures at their training medians, the estimated win probability is `r pct(probability_points$estimate[3])` at an equal gold difference, `r pct(probability_points$estimate[1])` at -4,000 gold, and `r pct(probability_points$estimate[5])` at +4,000 gold. The intervals at the extremes are wide (`r pct(probability_points$ci_low[1])` to `r pct(probability_points$ci_high[1])` at -4,000) because few training games sit there. These estimates are much less extreme than the raw band fractions of 0% and 100% in section 5.5, because the other three measures are fixed at median values here and the log odds are assumed to move linearly. The raw bands and this curve answer different questions, and the raw bands should not be read as win probabilities.

### 7.10 Saved outputs and what section 8 inherits

```{r save-baseline-artifacts}
saveRDS(list(baseline = baseline, baseline_formula = baseline_formula,
             reference_rate = reference_rate, coef_table = coef_table,
             step_table = step_table, vif_table = vif_table,
             separation_checks = separation_checks,
             binned_residuals = binned_residuals, flagged_bins = flagged_bins,
             spline_comparison = spline_comparison,
             influence_table = influence_table, coef_shift = coef_shift,
             team_residuals = team_residuals, week_residuals = week_residuals,
             score_table = score_table, calibration = calibration,
             probability_points = probability_points),
        file.path(artifact_dir, "baseline_logistic.rds"))
validation_rows <- score_table$set == "validation"
baseline_check <- list(
  scope = "section 7 (logistic regression baseline)", analysis_date = "2026-10-20",
  fitted_on = "initial training only", training_games = nrow(train),
  validation_games = nrow(validation), converged = isTRUE(baseline$converged),
  boundary_fit = isTRUE(baseline$boundary), max_vif = max(vif_table$vif),
  condition_number = condition_number,
  functional_form_bins_flagged = nrow(flagged_bins),
  predeclared_spline_comparison_run = form_problem,
  validation_log_loss = score_table$log_loss[validation_rows &
    score_table$model == "Four-predictor logistic regression"],
  reference_validation_log_loss = score_table$log_loss[validation_rows &
    score_table$model == "Training win-rate reference"],
  test_partitions_scored = FALSE, test_partitions_read = FALSE)
jsonlite::write_json(baseline_check, file.path(artifact_dir, "baseline_checks.json"),
                     pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)
```

Section 8 reuses the scoring functions from 7.1, the same outcome and predictors, the same training and validation games, and the reference forecast defined here. Three things carry forward. The linear functional form is kept. The validation log loss of `r sprintf("%.4f", score_table$log_loss[3])` is the number later models have to beat to justify their extra complexity. And sections 7.3 and 7.6 set an interpretation rule for the rest of the file: report predicted probabilities with their uncertainty, not individual coefficients. The two 2025 test sets stay untouched until the specification is frozen in section 9.
